passages.t: ‘God sent His Son’: no longer slaves but sons
passages.happening:
Paul gives a picture. A child who will one day own everything is, for now, “no different from a slave” (verse 1). He lives under guardians and trustees “until the date set by his father” (verse 2). “So also, when we were children, we were enslaved under the basic principles of the world” (verse 3).

Then the great turn. “But when the time had fully come, God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons” (verses 4-5).

“And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying out, ‘Abba, Father!’” (verse 6). “So you are no longer a slave, but a son; and since you are a son, you are also an heir through God” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Inheritance law shaped Paul's picture. In Greek and Roman households, a boy who stood to inherit an estate was put under guardians and managers until an age his father had fixed. On paper he owned it all. In daily life he had no more say than a household slave.

‘The basic principles of the world’ translates a Greek word that could mean the letters of the alphabet, the first lessons of a subject, or the elements of the world, earth, water, air and fire. Some writers used it for spirits linked to those elements. Paul seems to mean the old order that held people before Christ came: for Jews, life under the law as a guardian; for Gentiles, slavery to false gods. Readers differ on exactly what he meant.

‘When the time had fully come’: God chose the moment. Paul does not explain why then. He simply says the date set by the Father had arrived.

‘God sent His Son’ and ‘God sent the Spirit of His Son’ are the same verb. The Father sends the Son to do something for us, and sends the Spirit to do something in us. Here, in a letter written within about twenty-five years of the cross, the church's faith in the Father, the Son and the Spirit is already plain. Christians confess one God in three persons, not as a later idea but as what the Scriptures show.

‘Born of a woman, born under the law’ says that the Son became fully human, and a Jew, living under Israel's law. He shared the condition of those he came to rescue.

Adoption was a well-known Roman practice. A man, often one without an heir, could take another person as his son, with a new name and full rights to inherit. Paul says God has done this for believers.

Abba is the Aramaic word for father, the word Jesus used when he prayed in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). The Spirit leads Gentile believers, who spoke Greek, to pray to God with Jesus' own word.
passages.ot:
God called Israel his son long before. “When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son” (Hosea 11:1). He told Moses to say to Pharaoh, “Israel is My firstborn son” (Exodus 4:22). And through Jeremiah he grieved, “I thought you would call Me ‘Father’ and never turn away from following Me” (Jeremiah 3:19).

Paul hears in the Spirit's cry, ‘Abba, Father’, the answer to that longing. What God wanted from his people, he now gives by his Spirit.

‘Redeem’ is the word of the exodus. God brought Israel “out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2). Paul tells the story of salvation as a new exodus: slaves made free, and more than free, made sons and heirs.
passages.asks: Paul says the Spirit teaches believers to call God ‘Abba, Father’. Ask how you actually speak to God when you pray: as a slave hoping not to be punished, or as a child at home. If the word ‘father’ is painful because of your own father, it may help to know that God's fatherhood is not a copy of any human father's, good or bad. Ask what it would mean to pray to him as Jesus did.

passages.happening:
Paul reminds the Galatians where they came from. “Formerly, when you did not know God, you were slaves to those who by nature are not gods” (verse 8).

“But now that you know God, or rather are known by God, how is it that you are turning back to those weak and worthless principles? Do you wish to be enslaved by them all over again?” (verse 9).

“You are observing special days and months and seasons and years!” (verse 10). “I fear for you, that my efforts for you may have been in vain” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Before they believed, the Galatians had worshipped the gods of their cities, gods that Paul says are not gods at all. Every Galatian town had temples, festivals and a calendar of holy days for those gods.

Notice how Paul corrects himself: ‘you know God, or rather are known by God’. Knowing God starts with God. He knew them first.

Then a surprise. The teachers were urging the Galatians to keep the law of Moses, with its Sabbaths, new moons and festivals. Paul says that, for these Gentiles, taking up that calendar as a condition of belonging to Christ would be like going back to slavery. That sounds shocking, and he means it to. He is not saying that Israel's holy days were pagan. They were given by God. He is saying that, for people already set free in Christ, to make them the price of belonging is to go back under a guardian, and that the result would be a kind of slavery like the one they had left.

The ‘special days’ most likely means the Jewish calendar the teachers were pressing on them. Some readers think Paul chose words that would also fit the pagan calendars the Galatians had once kept, to show them the likeness.
passages.ot:
The holy days of Israel were God's gifts. The Sabbath was a sign of God's rest at creation and of his rescue from Egypt, and the feasts remembered what God had done. The Old Testament never calls them slavery.

Paul's point rests on the first commandment: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. You shall have no other gods before Me” (Exodus 20:2-3). The God who set Israel free is the God who has set the Galatians free. To go back to any kind of bondage, after that, is to forget the rescue.
passages.hard:
Does this mean Christians must not keep any holy days?

Paul's concern here is days kept as the price of belonging to Christ. Elsewhere he is relaxed about believers who choose to honour a day: “One person regards a certain day above the others, while someone else considers every day alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind” (Romans 14:5). Christians differ on these things. Most gather on Sunday, the day of the resurrection, and many keep Easter and Christmas. Some keep the seventh-day Sabbath. Some Jewish believers in Jesus keep the feasts of Israel. Paul's line is not at the calendar but at the gospel: no day kept or not kept makes anyone more fully a child of God. The site's note on Romans 14 sets out how he handles such differences.
passages.asks: Paul says the Galatians were known by God before they knew him. Ask what it means for you to be known by God, fully, and still welcomed. And ask whether there are habits, good in themselves, that you have turned into a way of proving you belong. Paul asks, ‘Do you wish to be enslaved by them all over again?’

passages.happening:
Now Paul pleads with them as a friend. “I beg you, brothers, become like me, for I became like you. You have done me no wrong” (verse 12).

He reminds them how they first met. “You know that it was because of an illness that I first preached the gospel to you” (verse 13). His illness was a trial to them, but they did not despise him. “Instead, you welcomed me as if I were an angel of God, as if I were Christ Jesus Himself” (verse 14). They would have torn out their own eyes and given them to him (verse 15).

“Have I now become your enemy by telling you the truth?” (verse 16). The other teachers are eager for them, “but not in a good way” (verse 17). They want to shut the Galatians out, so that the Galatians will be eager for them.

Then Paul cries out: “My children, for whom I am again in the pains of childbirth until Christ is formed in you, how I wish I could be with you now and change my tone, because I am perplexed about you” (verses 19-20).
passages.hearers:
‘Become like me, for I became like you’. Paul, a Jew, had lived among the Gentiles as one of them, free of the law's boundaries, so that they could know Christ. He asks them now to be free as he is.

Paul came to them sick. We do not know what the illness was. Some have guessed from verse 15 that it affected his eyes, and some link it with the ‘thorn in the flesh’ of 2 Corinthians 12, but these are guesses. ‘Torn out your eyes’ may simply be a way of saying they would have given him anything.

In Paul's world, sickness was sometimes taken as a sign that the gods were against a person. The Galatians could have turned away from a sick stranger. Instead they took him in as if he were Christ. Paul remembers that kindness, and it hurts him that it has cooled.

The other teachers, he says, are courting them. They ‘want to isolate you’, to shut the Galatians out of Paul's circle, so that the Galatians will depend on them.

Then Paul changes picture. He is like a mother in labour, again. He had given them birth once, when they came to faith. Now he is in pain again, ‘until Christ is formed in you’. It is a startling thing for a man to say of himself. It shows how much he loves them.
passages.ot:
Paul's picture of a mother in labour echoes the prophets, who used the same image for God's own work with his people. Through Isaiah God says, “Shall I bring a baby to the point of birth and not deliver it?” (Isaiah 66:9). Like God in Isaiah, Paul will not give up on the birth that has begun.

The Galatians' welcome of a sick stranger fits the hospitality Israel's law asked for: the stranger was to be loved, for Israel had been strangers in Egypt (Leviticus 19:34).
passages.asks: The Galatians once welcomed a sick, weak stranger as if he were Christ. Ask who is weak, sick or strange in your world, and how you receive them. And notice that Paul's sharp words come from a parent's pain. Ask whether the hard things you say to others come from love, and whether people can tell.

passages.t: Hagar and Sarah: the slave woman and the free
passages.happening:
“Tell me, you who want to be under the law, do you not understand what the law says?” (verse 21).

Paul tells the story of Abraham's two sons. One was born to Hagar, the slave woman, “according to the flesh”. The other was born to Sarah, the free woman, “through the promise” (verses 22-23).

Then he says plainly that he is using the story as a picture: “These things serve as illustrations, for the women represent two covenants” (verse 24). Hagar stands for Mount Sinai, and “corresponds to the present-day Jerusalem, because she is in slavery with her children” (verse 25). “But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (verse 26). Paul quotes Isaiah's song to the barren woman (verse 27).

“Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise” (verse 28). Then and now, the child born by the flesh persecuted the child born by the Spirit (verse 29). Paul quotes Sarah's words: “Expel the slave woman and her son” (verse 30). “Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman, but of the free woman” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
The teachers in Galatia loved the law. So Paul says: listen to what the law itself says. For Jews, ‘the law’ meant the first five books of the Bible, including Genesis. He takes them to the story of Abraham's sons.

Ishmael was born when Abraham and Sarah tried to make God's promise happen by their own plan, through Sarah's slave Hagar (Genesis 16). Isaac was born later, when Sarah was old and barren, only because God kept his word (Genesis 21). One birth came by human effort. The other came by promise.

Paul sets out two columns. On one side: Hagar, slavery, Ishmael born by the flesh, Mount Sinai, ‘the present-day Jerusalem’. On the other: Sarah, freedom, Isaac born by promise, ‘the Jerusalem above’. The Greek verb in verse 24 is the one from which the word ‘allegory’ comes. Paul tells his hearers that he is reading the story as a figure.

What is ‘the present-day Jerusalem’? Paul is writing about his own day and his own quarrel. The teachers in Galatia looked to Jerusalem for their authority, and pressed Gentiles to take on the law to belong. Many readers think ‘the present-day Jerusalem’ stands for that movement and its claims, the way of belonging by the law that the teachers offered. ‘The Jerusalem above’ is God's city, the people of God gathered by promise, Jew and Gentile. Paul calls her ‘our mother’.

‘Expel the slave woman’ may be Paul's way of telling the churches to stop listening to the teachers who would bring them into slavery. He is not telling anyone to drive people out of their homes.

Isaiah's song in verse 27 was first sung to Jerusalem in exile, desolate and childless. God promised her more children than she could count. Paul hears in it the many Gentiles now born into God's family.
passages.ot:
The story is from Genesis 16 and 21. Sarai, who had no children, gave her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abram, saying, “perhaps I can build a family by her” (Genesis 16:2). Later, after Isaac was born, Sarah saw Ishmael “mocking her son” and said, “Expel the slave woman and her son” (Genesis 21:9-10). Paul's quotation in verse 30 ends with ‘the free woman's son’, where Genesis has ‘my son Isaac’.

Isaiah 54:1 in the BSB reads, “Shout for joy, O barren woman, who bears no children” (Isaiah 54:1). Paul's ‘Rejoice’ follows the old Greek translation. In Isaiah the song follows the chapter of the suffering servant (Isaiah 53). The servant's suffering brings the barren city her children.

The picture of Zion as a mother of many peoples is in the Psalms too: “This one and that one were born in her” (Psalm 87:5). And Isaiah saw the nations coming to her, saying, “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD” (Isaiah 2:3).

The notes on Genesis 16 and 21 in this Study Bible tell Hagar's story in its own place.
passages.hard:
Paul's picture of Hagar and Sarah has been badly misused, and it has to be read with care.

First, it is not a verdict on Hagar. In Genesis, Hagar is a woman treated harshly, whom God sees, names and blesses (Genesis 16 and 21). Paul does not retell her story; he uses it as a figure in an argument, and he says so. The site's note on Genesis 16:13-16 says more about Hagar, and about Ishmael, who is honoured by Muslims.

Second, it is not a verdict on the Jewish people. Paul is a Jew, writing about a quarrel among Jewish believers in Jesus over whether Gentiles must keep the law. ‘The present-day Jerusalem’ points to the way of belonging that the teachers in Galatia were pressing, not to Jews as a people, then or now. The same Paul writes, “did God reject His people? Certainly not!” (Romans 11:1). The law given at Sinai was God's good gift (Romans 7:12).

For centuries some Christians used this passage, and others like it, to teach contempt for Jews and to justify cruelty against them. That reading is false, and Christians must reject it plainly. This site rejects it. The note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out why.

Third, ‘the son born by the flesh persecuted the son born by the Spirit’ (verse 29) describes how the teachers were treating the Galatian believers, and the pressure Paul himself faced. It gives no one licence to treat anyone as an enemy.

Paul's point is about two ways of belonging to God: by human effort, which ends in slavery, or by God's promise, which brings freedom. Every believer, Jewish or Gentile, belongs by promise.
passages.asks: Abraham and Sarah once tried to make God's promise happen by their own plan, and much pain followed. Ask where you are trying to make God's promises come true by your own effort. And ask what it means to live as a child of the free woman: not anxious to earn your place, but secure in a promise God has kept.
